title: Human Genetics (ANA 341)
description: Chromosomes and karyotyping, patterns of inheritance, chromosomal disorders, genetic diseases common in Nigeria, and genetic counselling.

topics.title: Chromosomes and Karyotyping
topics.summary: Human chromosome complement, chromosome structure, karyotype analysis and nomenclature.

notes.b: Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). Chromosomes are classified by centromere position: metacentric (central), submetacentric, acrocentric (near one end — chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, 22, prone to Robertsonian translocations) and telocentric (not normally seen in humans). The short arm is 'p' and the long arm 'q'. The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene, which determines male development.
k: p = short arm; q = long arm

notes.b: A karyotype is prepared from dividing cells (usually cultured lymphocytes stimulated with phytohaemagglutinin) arrested in metaphase with colchicine, then stained (G-banding with Giemsa). Normal karyotypes are written 46,XX or 46,XY; Down syndrome 47,XX,+21; Turner syndrome 45,X; Klinefelter 47,XXY. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) and chromosomal microarray detect smaller deletions and duplications. The Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome seen in female somatic cells (number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1; Lyon hypothesis).

topics.title: Patterns of Single-Gene Inheritance
topics.summary: Autosomal dominant and recessive, X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance with pedigrees.

notes.b: Autosomal dominant (AD) disorders appear in every generation, affect both sexes equally, and an affected heterozygote has a 50% chance of passing the condition to each child; examples: achondroplasia, Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolaemia, neurofibromatosis type 1, polycystic kidney disease (adult). Autosomal recessive (AR) disorders often skip generations, affect both sexes, and two carrier parents have a 25% risk per pregnancy of an affected child; consanguinity increases risk. Examples: sickle cell disease, albinism, cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, thalassaemia, Tay–Sachs disease.
k: Sickle cell and albinism are AR

notes.b: X-linked recessive disorders mainly affect males; there is no male-to-male transmission; carrier mothers pass the condition to 50% of sons, and 50% of daughters are carriers; all daughters of an affected man are carriers. Examples: haemophilia A and B, G6PD deficiency, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, red–green colour blindness. X-linked dominant disorders (e.g. vitamin D-resistant rickets) pass from an affected father to all daughters and no sons. Mitochondrial disorders are inherited only from the mother. Concepts: penetrance (proportion of genotype carriers who show the phenotype), expressivity (variation in severity), anticipation (earlier/worse in successive generations — trinucleotide repeat disorders such as Huntington disease).
k: X-linked recessive: males affected, no male-to-male transmission

topics.title: Chromosomal Disorders
topics.summary: Trisomies, sex chromosome aneuploidies, deletions and translocations.

notes.b: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), the commonest chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, is usually due to maternal meiotic non-disjunction (risk rises with maternal age); about 4% arise from Robertsonian translocation (e.g. 14;21) and may recur in families. Features: flat face, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar crease, sandal gap, hypotonia, congenital heart disease (atrioventricular septal defect), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism and early Alzheimer disease, with increased leukaemia risk. Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18): clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia. Patau syndrome (trisomy 13): cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly.
k: Down: trisomy 21, maternal age, AVSD, duodenal atresia
Edwards: trisomy 18, clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet

notes.b: Turner syndrome (45,X): short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, lymphoedema at birth, streak ovaries with primary amenorrhoea and infertility, coarctation of the aorta, normal intelligence. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): tall stature, small testes, gynaecomastia, infertility (azoospermia), raised FSH/LH. Structural abnormalities include deletions (cri-du-chat — 5p deletion, cat-like cry), duplications, inversions and translocations; the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) forms the BCR-ABL fusion gene in chronic myeloid leukaemia.
k: Turner: short, webbed neck, coarctation, streak ovaries

topics.title: Molecular Genetics and Mutations
topics.summary: Gene structure, types of mutations, DNA repair defects and molecular diagnostic tools.

notes.b: Point mutations include silent (no amino acid change), missense (one amino acid changed — e.g. HbS: GAG → GTG, glutamic acid to valine at β6) and nonsense (premature stop codon, e.g. some β-thalassaemias). Insertions or deletions not in multiples of three cause frameshifts (e.g. Tay–Sachs, many Duchenne muscular dystrophy cases). Trinucleotide repeat expansions cause fragile X syndrome (CGG), Huntington disease (CAG) and myotonic dystrophy (CTG). Splice-site mutations alter mRNA processing (some β-thalassaemias). Mutagens include ionising and UV radiation, chemicals and some viruses.

The polymerase chain reaction (PCR; Kary Mullis) amplifies DNA through cycles of denaturation (~94 °C), annealing of primers (~50–65 °C) and extension (~72 °C) by heat-stable Taq polymerase. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size (smaller move faster). Sanger sequencing and next-generation sequencing read DNA sequences. Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites; RFLP analysis was historically used to detect the sickle mutation (loss of an MstII site). Southern blotting detects DNA, Northern RNA, and Western proteins. Haemoglobin electrophoresis and HPLC are routine for sickle cell diagnosis.
k: Southern DNA, Northern RNA, Western protein

topics.title: Genetic Disorders in Nigeria and Genetic Counselling
topics.summary: Sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency, albinism and thalassaemia; prevention and counselling.

notes.b: Nigeria has the world's largest burden of sickle cell disease: about 20–25% of adults carry HbS (AS genotype), and an estimated 150,000 babies are born with SCD each year. HbSC disease is also common. Diagnosis uses haemoglobin electrophoresis, HPLC or point-of-care tests; newborn screening enables early penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination. Hydroxyurea increases HbF and reduces crises. G6PD deficiency (X-linked) is common and causes haemolysis with oxidant drugs and infections. Oculocutaneous albinism (AR) is relatively frequent; affected people need sun protection because of high skin cancer risk, and eye care for low vision.
k: Albinism: sun protection, skin cancer risk

notes.b: Genetic counselling helps individuals and families understand the risk, inheritance, implications and options regarding genetic conditions. It should be non-directive, confidential and culturally sensitive. Prevention strategies include premarital and preconception genotype screening, carrier testing, prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling at 10–13 weeks, amniocentesis at 15–20 weeks), and preimplantation genetic diagnosis with IVF. Pedigree charts use squares for males, circles for females, shaded symbols for affected persons, half-shaded or dotted symbols for carriers, and a double line for consanguineous unions.
